questions.stem: A 36 year old woman has 6 months of tiredness and a sore tongue. Her periods are heavy and last 8 days. She has pale conjunctivae and a smooth, red tongue. Her pulse rate is 96 bpm. Investigations are shown.
questions.q: Which is the most likely additional finding on examination?
questions.e: Koilonychia (spoon-shaped nails) is a classic sign of iron deficiency, the commonest microcytic anaemia, here from menorrhagia.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
Microcytic anaemia with menorrhagia.

elim: A feature of haemolysis, not iron deficiency.
Points to B12 deficiency, which causes a macrocytic anaemia.
Suggests haemolysis or a haematological malignancy.
Hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia; no history of nosebleeds or family history.

steps.x: **B. Koilonychia.** Iron deficiency: koilonychia, glossitis, pallor.

questions.stem: A 42 year old woman has 4 months of tiredness and breathlessness on exertion. She has had heavy periods for a year. Her pulse rate is 98 bpm. She has pale conjunctivae. Haemoglobin is 92 g/L (115–165) and MCV is 70 fL (80–100). Iron studies are requested.
questions.q: Which pattern of iron studies is most likely?
o: High ferritin, high iron, high transferrin saturation
Low ferritin, high TIBC, low transferrin saturation
Low ferritin, low TIBC, high transferrin saturation
Normal ferritin, low TIBC, low transferrin saturation
Normal ferritin, normal TIBC, normal transferrin saturation
questions.e: Iron deficiency gives low ferritin, low transferrin saturation and a high TIBC as the body tries to capture more iron.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
Microcytic anaemia from chronic blood loss.

elim: Sideroblastic anaemia or iron overload.
Not a recognised pattern.
Anaemia of chronic disease.
Would not fit a microcytic anaemia from blood loss.

steps.x: **B. Low ferritin, high TIBC, low transferrin saturation.** IDA: ferritin low, TIBC high, saturation low.

questions.stem: A 69 year old man with stage 4 chronic kidney disease from diabetic nephropathy has 6 months of tiredness. He has no bleeding or change in bowel habit. His pulse rate is 84 bpm. Investigations are shown.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his anaemia?
questions.e: A normocytic anaemia (MCV 80–100) with normal ferritin in CKD is the anaemia of chronic disease/CKD, from reduced erythropoietin and inflammation.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
Normocytic anaemia with normal ferritin in CKD.

elim: White cells and platelets are normal.
Bilirubin and reticulocytes would be raised.
Ferritin is normal and the MCV is normal, not low.
Causes macrocytosis; his MCV is normal.

steps.x: **A. Anaemia of chronic kidney disease.** Normocytic: chronic disease, CKD, acute blood loss.

questions.stem: A 34 year old woman has followed a strict vegan diet for 8 years without supplements. She has 3 months of tiredness, tingling in both feet and unsteadiness in the dark. Vibration sense is reduced at the ankles and Romberg's test is positive. Investigations are shown.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: B12 deficiency causes a macrocytic anaemia and, unlike folate deficiency, neurological features such as neuropathy and dorsal column loss; a vegan diet lacks B12.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
Macrocytic anaemia with neurology in someone who eats no animal products.

elim: She does not drink heavily, and it does not explain dorsal column signs.
Also macrocytic, but does not cause neurological signs.
Gives a non-megaloblastic macrocytosis without dorsal column loss.
Occurs in older people and does not cause neuropathy.

steps.x: **E. Vitamin B12 deficiency.** Macrocytic + neuro = B12, not folate.

questions.stem: A 58 year old man drinks heavily and eats very little apart from bread. He has 2 months of tiredness and breathlessness. Neurological examination is normal, with normal vibration and joint position sense. Serum B12 is normal. Investigations are shown.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his anaemia?
questions.e: A macrocytic anaemia with a poor diet, normal B12 and no neurology is folate deficiency.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.

clues: eats very little apart from bread
steps.x: Macrocytic anaemia without neurology and a normal B12.

elim: Causes a microcytic, not macrocytic, anaemia.
Causes low B12, which is normal here.
Usually microcytic with ring sideroblasts.
Causes microcytosis.

steps.x: **A. Folate deficiency.** Macrocytic, no neurology, poor diet = folate.

questions.stem: A 54 year old woman has 6 months of tiredness, weight gain, dry skin and thinning hair. She finds it hard to climb stairs. She drinks no alcohol and eats a varied diet. Investigations show haemoglobin 108 g/L (115–165), MCV 104 fL (80–100), normal B12 and folate, and no hypersegmented neutrophils on film.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her macrocytic anaemia?
questions.e: Non-megaloblastic macrocytosis with tiredness, weight gain, proximal myopathy, dry skin and thin hair is mainly due to hypothyroidism.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.

clues: weight gain, dry skin and thinning hair
steps.x: Non-megaloblastic macrocytosis with hypothyroid features.

elim: She drinks none.
Folate is normal.
Possible in older people but does not explain weight gain, dry skin and proximal weakness.
B12 is normal and the film is not megaloblastic.

steps.x: **C. Hypothyroidism.** Macrocytic, normal B12/folate, hypothyroid features = check TFTs.

questions.stem: A 27 year old man has 2 weeks of tiredness and yellow eyes. His urine is normal in colour. He is jaundiced with a palpable spleen tip. His pulse rate is 100 bpm. Investigations are shown.
questions.q: Which type of anaemia is most likely?
questions.e: Anaemia with jaundice, splenomegaly, raised unconjugated bilirubin, high LDH and a high reticulocyte count is haemolysis.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.

clues: jaundiced with a palpable spleen tip
steps.x: Anaemia + jaundice + splenomegaly + reticulocytosis.

elim: Does not cause jaundice, splenomegaly and reticulocytosis.
Reticulocytes would be low with pancytopenia.
Microcytic, without jaundice.
Can raise LDH but reticulocytes are low, and it is macrocytic.

steps.x: **C. Haemolytic anaemia.** Haemolysis: high retics, LDH, unconjugated bilirubin.

questions.stem: A 38 year old woman has 3 days of fever, headache and confusion. She has bruises on her legs and passes little urine. Her temperature is 38.4°C, pulse rate 108 bpm and BP 146/90 mmHg. She has a transient right arm weakness. Blood film shows schistocytes. Investigations are shown.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: TTP pentad: fever, microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia (schistocytes), thrombocytopenia, AKI and neurological features.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
Fever, neurology, MAHA, low platelets and AKI.

elim: Shows spherocytes and a positive DAT, not schistocytes with low platelets and neurology.
Clotting times would be prolonged; they are normal.
Usually a child after bloody diarrhoea, without prominent neurology.
Low platelets but no haemolysis or renal failure.

steps.x: **E. Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura.** TTP = the pentad; HUS = triad in a child after diarrhoea.

questions.stem: A 5 year old boy had bloody diarrhoea 6 days ago after a farm visit. He is now pale, lethargic and passing very little urine. He has no seizures or focal neurology. His pulse rate is 130 bpm and BP 118/76 mmHg. Blood film shows fragmented red cells. Investigations are shown.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: HUS triad: haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia and AKI (creatinine about twice baseline), classically after E. coli O157 diarrhoea in a child.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.

clues: bloody diarrhoea 6 days ago after a farm visit
steps.x: Child, post-diarrhoeal, MAHA with renal failure.

elim: Palpable purpura with a normal platelet count.
Spherocytes, not fragments, and no renal failure.
Isolated thrombocytopenia without haemolysis.
Usually an adult with fever and neurology.

steps.x: **A. Haemolytic uraemic syndrome.** HUS = haemolysis + low platelets + AKI after diarrhoea.

questions.stem: A 41 year old man has been taking isoniazid for latent tuberculosis for 4 months without pyridoxine. He has 6 weeks of tiredness. His pulse rate is 94 bpm. Blood film shows hypochromic cells and Pappenheimer bodies. Bone marrow shows ring sideroblasts. Investigations are shown.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Sideroblastic anaemia mimics iron deficiency (hypochromic, microcytic) but iron and ferritin are high; ring sideroblasts and Pappenheimer bodies are seen. Isoniazid without pyridoxine is a cause.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
Microcytic anaemia with high iron stores.

elim: Normocytic, with low serum iron.
Microcytic with normal iron and no ring sideroblasts.
Ferritin would be low, not high.
Lead can cause it, but he is anaemic and the cause is isoniazid.

steps.x: **E. Sideroblastic anaemia.** Microcytic + high ferritin + ring sideroblasts = sideroblastic.

questions.stem: A 9 year old girl had a bright red rash on both cheeks 3 weeks ago. She is now pale and tired and has had two nosebleeds and a chest infection. She has petechiae on her legs. There is no lymphadenopathy or splenomegaly. Her pulse rate is 120 bpm. Investigations are shown.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Aplastic anaemia is stem-cell failure giving pancytopenia; it can follow a viral illness, classically parvovirus B19 (slapped cheek).

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.

clues: bright red rash on both cheeks
steps.x: Pancytopenia after a slapped cheek illness.

elim: Usually with lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly and blasts on film.
Follows diarrhoea and causes AKI with a normal white count.
Isolated low platelets, not pancytopenia.
Does not cause neutropenia and low platelets.

steps.x: **B. Aplastic anaemia.** Pancytopenia after parvovirus = aplastic anaemia.

questions.stem: A 31 year old woman is 30 weeks pregnant and has taken methyldopa for hypertension for 10 weeks. She has 2 weeks of tiredness and mild jaundice. She has no fever or bloody diarrhoea. Blood film shows spherocytes. Investigations are shown.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Warm AIHA is the commonest type: IgG autoantibodies, positive DAT, spherocytes, often drug-induced (methyldopa, cephalosporins, NSAIDs, ciprofloxacin).

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
DAT-positive haemolysis with spherocytes on a known culprit drug.

elim: IgM, linked to Mycoplasma and lymphoma, worse in the cold.
Bite cells and Heinz bodies with a negative DAT.
Spherocytes but a negative DAT and a lifelong family history.
Schistocytes and low platelets.

steps.x: **E. Warm autoimmune haemolytic anaemia.** Methyldopa + DAT positive (IgG) = warm AIHA.

questions.stem: A 23 year old man from Ghana is given primaquine to prevent malaria relapse. Four days later he is tired, jaundiced and passing dark urine. His pulse rate is 104 bpm. Haemoglobin has fallen from 148 to 98 g/L (130–180). The direct antiglobulin test is negative.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on his blood film?
questions.e: G6PD deficiency causes oxidant-triggered haemolysis (primaquine, nitrofurantoin, fava beans); Heinz bodies form and the spleen removes them, leaving bite cells.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
Acute DAT-negative haemolysis after an oxidant drug.

elim: Megaloblastic anaemia (B12 or folate deficiency).
Iron deficiency.
Hereditary spherocytosis or warm AIHA.
Thalassaemia, liver disease or hyposplenism.

steps.x: **A. Bite cells.** G6PD: Heinz bodies and bite cells.

questions.stem: A 71 year old woman had a mechanical mitral valve replacement 3 years ago. She has 3 months of tiredness and her urine is sometimes dark. She is mildly jaundiced. Her pulse rate is 92 bpm and she has a loud metallic click. Haemoglobin is 94 g/L (115–165), LDH is 780 U/L (120–250) and the direct antiglobulin test is negative.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on her blood film?
questions.e: A mechanical valve shears red cells, causing acquired DAT-negative haemolysis with schistocytes (fragmented cells).

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
Haemolysis with a prosthetic valve.

elim: Oxidative damage in G6PD deficiency.
Seen after splenectomy.
Seen in bone marrow in sideroblastic anaemia.
Warm AIHA or hereditary spherocytosis.

steps.x: **D. Schistocytes.** Mechanical valve haemolysis = schistocytes.

questions.stem: A 47 year old woman attends for a routine blood test and has a haemoglobin of 72 g/L (115–165) with an MCV of 66 fL (80–100). She has had heavy periods for 2 years. She says she feels only a little tired and still walks her dog daily. Her pulse rate is 88 bpm and BP 122/76 mmHg.
questions.q: Which best explains why her symptoms are so mild?
o: Her haemoglobin result is falsely low
She has a high reticulocyte count
Women need less haemoglobin than men
questions.e: Anaemia reduces oxygen-carrying capacity; symptoms depend on severity and speed of onset, and slow loss allows compensation.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
Severe but gradual anaemia.

elim: No reason to suspect error; the MCV is also abnormal.
It causes fatigue, breathlessness and palpitations.
Iron deficiency gives a low reticulocyte response.
Reference ranges differ, but 72 g/L is markedly low for anyone.

steps.x: **D. The anaemia developed slowly.** Slow anaemia is well tolerated; fast anaemia is not.

questions.stem: A 62 year old woman with type 1 diabetes and vitiligo has 4 months of tiredness and a sore tongue. Haemoglobin is 92 g/L (115–165), MCV 116 fL (80–100) and serum B12 is 88 ng/L (180–900). She eats meat daily and has had no bowel surgery.
questions.q: Which test is most specific for the likely cause?
questions.e: Pernicious anaemia is autoimmune B12 deficiency from antibodies against intrinsic factor and parietal cells; intrinsic factor antibodies are the specific test.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what test answers the clinical question being asked.
B12 deficiency despite a good diet, with other autoimmune disease.

elim: Coeliac disease affects folate and iron more than B12.
For autoimmune haemolysis.
More sensitive but much less specific.
Does not explain a macrocytic B12-deficient anaemia.

steps.x: **D. Intrinsic factor antibodies.** Pernicious anaemia: intrinsic factor antibodies.

questions.stem: A 39 year old woman has tiredness and heavy periods. Haemoglobin is 104 g/L (115–165) and MCV 77 fL (80–100). CRP is 3 mg/L (<5). She has no chronic illness. Her GP wants a single blood result that confirms iron deficiency.
questions.q: Which result would confirm iron deficiency anaemia?
questions.e: Iron deficiency anaemia is diagnosed by a serum ferritin below 30 µg/L in a patient without inflammation.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what test answers the clinical question being asked.
Confirming low iron stores with no inflammation.

elim: Iron would be low; it also varies through the day.
Seen in haemolysis or bleeding with intact iron stores.
Suggests iron overload or inflammation.
Suggests iron overload.

steps.x: **D. Serum ferritin below 30 µg/L.** Ferritin <30 µg/L confirms iron deficiency.

questions.stem: A 64 year old man with non-Hodgkin lymphoma has 2 weeks of tiredness and jaundice. His spleen is enlarged. Haemoglobin is 82 g/L (130–180), reticulocytes 7% (0.5–2.5), LDH 610 U/L (120–250) and the blood film shows spherocytes. He has no family history of anaemia.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
questions.e: A positive direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test confirms autoimmune haemolytic anaemia; lymphoproliferative disease is a classic cause of warm AIHA.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what test answers the clinical question being asked.
Acquired spherocytic haemolysis in lymphoma.

elim: Not needed to confirm autoimmune haemolysis.
G6PD shows bite cells, not spherocytes.
For thalassaemia and sickle cell disease.
For hereditary spherocytosis, which has a family history.

steps.x: **B. Direct antiglobulin test.** Spherocytes + lymphoma: DAT (Coombs) test.

questions.stem: A 73 year old woman has iron deficiency anaemia: haemoglobin 98 g/L (115–165), MCV 72 fL (80–100) and ferritin 9 µg/L (30–400). She has no bowel symptoms. A faecal immunochemical test (FIT) is positive.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step?
o: Oral iron and no further investigation
Refer on the suspected cancer pathway
questions.e: Patients over 60 with iron deficiency anaemia need investigation for colorectal cancer; a positive FIT means referral on the suspected cancer pathway.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what test answers the clinical question being asked.
Older patient with IDA and a positive FIT.

elim: Reasonable to add, but a positive FIT needs urgent referral.
Misses a possible colorectal cancer.
Delays diagnosis.
A positive FIT needs the urgent suspected cancer pathway.

steps.x: **C. Refer on the suspected cancer pathway.** Over 60 with IDA: FIT; positive = urgent referral.

questions.stem: A 21 year old woman has 1 week of tiredness and yellow eyes after a viral illness. Haemoglobin is 98 g/L (115–165) with an MCV of 101 fL (80–100). Her bilirubin is raised, mainly unconjugated. Her GP wants a test that shows the marrow is responding to red cell loss.
questions.q: Which result would most support haemolysis?
questions.e: The marrow compensates for haemolysis with reticulocytosis, which can also nudge the MCV up; raised LDH and unconjugated bilirubin support it.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what test answers the clinical question being asked.
Evidence of marrow compensation.

elim: LDH is raised in haemolysis.
Would suggest megaloblastic anaemia.
Points to liver or biliary disease.
Non-specific.

steps.x: **D. Raised reticulocyte count.** Haemolysis: retics up, LDH up, unconjugated bilirubin up.

questions.stem: A 67 year old woman has 2 months of tiredness, bruising and mouth ulcers. She has no lymphadenopathy or splenomegaly. Haemoglobin is 74 g/L (115–165), white cells 1.4 ×10⁹/L (4.0–11.0), platelets 16 ×10⁹/L (150–400) and reticulocytes are low. The blood film shows no blasts. A bone marrow aspirate gives a dry tap with very few cells.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis?
o: CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis
Repeat full blood count in 3 months
questions.e: Aplastic anaemia is investigated with bone marrow aspiration, with trephine biopsy as the confirmatory test showing a hypocellular, fatty marrow.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what test answers the clinical question being asked.

clues: dry tap with very few cells
steps.x: Pancytopenia with an inadequate aspirate.

elim: Looks for lymphoma, but there is no lymphadenopathy and it cannot assess marrow cellularity.
For autoimmune haemolysis, which would give a high reticulocyte count.
Delays diagnosis of a dangerous pancytopenia.
Does not explain pancytopenia.

steps.x: **A. Bone marrow trephine biopsy.** Aplastic anaemia: aspirate, then trephine biopsy to confirm.

questions.stem: A 52 year old woman has warm autoimmune haemolytic anaemia. She is tired and mildly jaundiced. Her pulse rate is 96 bpm and BP 124/76 mmHg. Haemoglobin is 84 g/L (115–165) and the direct antiglobulin test is positive for IgG. She is not taking any new medicines.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial treatment?
questions.e: Warm AIHA is treated first with steroids (prednisolone), with transfusion if needed, ± rituximab; immunosuppressants and splenectomy are second-line.

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs now, at this point in the pathway.
Stable warm AIHA needing first-line immunosuppression.

elim: She is not iron deficient; this is immune destruction.
Used for TTP and severe cold AIHA.
An add-on or second-line, not the first step.
Second-line if steroids and other treatments fail.

steps.x: **B. Oral prednisolone.** Warm AIHA: prednisolone first.

questions.stem: A 68 year old man has cold autoimmune haemolytic anaemia with lymphoma. He has had severe haemolytic episodes despite keeping warm, and haemoglobin has fallen to 62 g/L (130–180) with dark urine. His fingers turn white in the cold. The haematologist wants to rapidly remove the circulating IgM antibody.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.e: In severe cold AIHA, plasmapheresis removes circulating IgM; keeping warm and treating the cause (lymphoma) also matter.

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs now, at this point in the pathway.
Severe cold agglutinin disease.

elim: Steroids work poorly in cold AIHA.
Not iron deficient.
Ineffective, as cold AIHA causes mainly intravascular haemolysis.
The high MCV reflects reticulocytes, not B12 deficiency.

steps.x: **C. Plasmapheresis.** Severe cold AIHA: plasmapheresis.

questions.stem: A 33 year old woman is diagnosed with thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura. She has fever, confusion, platelets of 12 ×10⁹/L (150–400), schistocytes on film and a raised creatinine. Clotting is normal. She has no active bleeding.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate urgent treatment?
questions.e: Microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia from TTP is treated urgently with plasma exchange, which removes the antibody and replaces ADAMTS13.

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs now, at this point in the pathway.
TTP: a medical emergency.

elim: Not the treatment for TTP.
Steroids may be added, but plasma exchange is the key treatment.
Can worsen microthrombi and is avoided unless life-threatening bleeding.
Not an urgent treatment for TTP.

steps.x: **C. Plasma exchange.** TTP: plasma exchange; avoid platelets.

questions.stem: A 66 year old woman with iron deficiency anaemia is listed for an elective hip replacement in 10 weeks. Haemoglobin is 104 g/L (115–165) and ferritin 14 µg/L (30–400). Her colonoscopy and gastroscopy were normal. She has never taken iron before and has no gut symptoms.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate treatment before surgery?
questions.e: Before surgery, oral iron is used if there are more than 6 weeks until the operation; IV iron is used if under 6 weeks.

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs now, at this point in the pathway.
Time to correct iron deficiency orally.

elim: She is stable and has time to correct iron.
Used when surgery is less than 6 weeks away or oral iron fails.
Not needed; iron can be replaced in time.
She is iron deficient, not B12 deficient.

steps.x: **C. Oral iron.** More than 6 weeks to surgery: oral iron.

questions.stem: A 45 year old man with Crohn's disease has iron deficiency anaemia. Haemoglobin is 92 g/L (130–180) and ferritin 8 µg/L (30–400). He has tried daily and then alternate-day oral ferrous fumarate with a laxative for 3 months but could not tolerate it, and his haemoglobin has not risen.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step?
o: Stop iron and recheck in 6 months
questions.e: IV iron is second-line for iron deficiency anaemia when oral iron is not tolerated or ineffective (for example in inflammatory bowel disease).

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs now, at this point in the pathway.
Oral iron has failed.

elim: He is stable; transfusion is for haemodynamic instability.
Worsens side effects and he cannot tolerate it.
Not iron deficiency treatment.
Leaves him anaemic.

steps.x: **D. Intravenous iron.** Oral iron fails → IV iron.

questions.stem: A 79 year old man with myelodysplasia and normocytic anaemia attends the day unit. He is breathless walking to the bathroom. His pulse rate is 98 bpm and BP 128/70 mmHg. Haemoglobin is 64 g/L (130–180) and MCV 94 fL (80–100). He has no heart failure. A transfusion is planned.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate transfusion plan?
o: Transfuse 1 unit only if haemoglobin falls below 50 g/L
questions.e: In normocytic anaemia, transfuse 1 unit of red cells at a time to maintain Hb above 70 g/L where indicated, reassessing after each unit.

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs now, at this point in the pathway.
Symptomatic anaemia below 70 g/L in an elderly patient.

elim: He is symptomatic and below the 70 g/L threshold now.
Over-transfusion risks fluid overload in an elderly man.
Aims far above the target and risks overload.
Platelets are not the problem.

steps.x: **A. Transfuse 1 unit and reassess.** One unit, then reassess; target Hb >70.

questions.stem: A 7 year old boy of English descent has hereditary spherocytosis. His father has it too. He needs blood transfusions every few months for haemoglobin below 60 g/L, has had gallstones and has a large spleen. He is fully vaccinated.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive management?
questions.e: Hereditary spherocytosis (autosomal dominant, Northern Europeans) is managed in severe cases with childhood splenectomy, after vaccination.

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs now, at this point in the pathway.
Severe transfusion-dependent spherocytosis.

elim: Not used for hereditary spherocytosis.
He is not iron deficient and transfusion adds iron.
For autoimmune haemolysis, not a membrane defect.
For TTP and severe cold AIHA.

steps.x: **E. Splenectomy.** Severe HS: splenectomy.

questions.stem: A 70 year old man has a new iron deficiency anaemia: haemoglobin 108 g/L (130–180), MCV 74 fL (80–100), ferritin 12 µg/L (30–400). He eats a normal diet. He feels well and asks if he can just take iron tablets and avoid tests.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate approach?
o: Iron tablets only and repeat bloods in a year
Reassure; this is normal for his age
Start iron and investigate the cause
questions.e: The general approach to anaemia is to investigate the cause and treat it; in someone over 60 that means looking for colorectal cancer.

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs now, at this point in the pathway.
Unexplained IDA in an older man.

elim: Misses a GI cancer.
Iron deficiency in an older man is never normal.
He is stable and well.
He is iron, not B12, deficient.

steps.x: **C. Start iron and investigate the cause.** Treat the anaemia AND find the cause.

questions.stem: A 30 year old woman has iron deficiency anaemia from menorrhagia. Her blood film shows small, pale red cells with an MCV of 68 fL (80–100) and a low MCH. She asks why lack of iron makes her red cells small and pale.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism?
questions.e: Iron is needed for haem; without it, erythroid precursors are under-haemoglobinised and cells are small (microcytic) and pale (hypochromic).

steps.x: A science question: explain the finding with the underlying mechanism.
Too little haemoglobin made per cell.

elim: Causes large megaloblastic cells in B12/folate deficiency.
Haemolysis; cells are not typically small and pale.
Hereditary spherocytosis.
Thalassaemia, a different cause of microcytosis.

steps.x: **E. Reduced haem synthesis.** Iron deficiency → less haem → microcytic, hypochromic.

questions.stem: A 19 year old man with hereditary spherocytosis has a viral illness and becomes jaundiced. His urine is a normal colour, ALT is normal and haemoglobin has fallen to 98 g/L (130–180). A student asks why his skin is yellow.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his jaundice?
questions.e: Premature red cell destruction releases haem, which is metabolised to unconjugated bilirubin; it is not water soluble, so urine stays normal (acholuric jaundice).

steps.x: A science question: explain the finding with the underlying mechanism.
Prehepatic jaundice during haemolysis.

elim: Gives conjugated bilirubin with dark urine and pale stools.
ALT is normal.
Would not cause a fall in haemoglobin.
Does not cause yellow sclerae or anaemia.

steps.x: **C. Haem breakdown to unconjugated bilirubin.** Haemolysis = unconjugated bilirubin, acholuric jaundice.

questions.stem: A 28 year old man with G6PD deficiency has acute haemolysis after eating fava beans. His blood film shows red cells that look as though a semicircle has been bitten out of their edge. A supravital stain shows inclusions inside some cells.
questions.q: Which best explains the appearance of these cells?
questions.e: Oxidative stress denatures haemoglobin into Heinz bodies; splenic macrophages pluck them out, leaving bite cells.

steps.x: A science question: explain the finding with the underlying mechanism.
Oxidised haemoglobin is removed by the spleen.

elim: Gives spherocytes in warm AIHA.
Gives schistocytes.
Gives spherocytes in hereditary spherocytosis.
Howell-Jolly bodies after splenectomy.

steps.x: **E. Splenic removal of Heinz bodies.** Heinz bodies → spleen removes → bite cells.

questions.stem: A 60 year old woman with chronic lymphocytic leukaemia has warm autoimmune haemolytic anaemia. Her spleen is enlarged, her urine is a normal colour and the blood film shows spherocytes. The direct antiglobulin test is positive for IgG.
questions.q: Where are her red cells mainly destroyed?
questions.e: In warm (IgG) AIHA, antibody-coated cells are removed extravascularly by splenic macrophages, which nibble membrane and leave spherocytes.

steps.x: A science question: explain the finding with the underlying mechanism.
IgG haemolysis with splenomegaly and spherocytes.

elim: The marrow is producing more cells, not destroying them.
Typical of cold IgM AIHA.
Not a site of red cell destruction.
Microangiopathic haemolysis.

steps.x: **E. Splenic macrophages.** Warm IgG AIHA = extravascular, spleen, spherocytes.

questions.stem: A 24 year old woman had Mycoplasma pneumonia 2 weeks ago. Since the weather turned cold she has had episodes of passing red-brown urine, and her fingers turn white and numb outdoors. The direct antiglobulin test is positive for complement (C3d). Haemoglobin is 92 g/L (115–165).
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her haemolysis?
o: IgM fixing complement in the cold
questions.e: Cold AIHA: IgM antibodies (after Mycoplasma or with lymphoma) bind at low temperatures and fix complement, causing more intravascular haemolysis (haemoglobinuria) and Raynaud's.

steps.x: A science question: explain the finding with the underlying mechanism.
Cold-triggered intravascular haemolysis after Mycoplasma.

elim: Oxidant-triggered with a negative DAT.
Warm AIHA, which is extravascular.
Microangiopathic haemolysis.
Hereditary spherocytosis.

steps.x: **C. IgM fixing complement in the cold.** Cold AIHA = IgM + complement = intravascular.

questions.stem: A 26 year old man has aplastic anaemia after a viral hepatitis. He has recurrent infections, gum bleeding and tiredness. White cells, platelets, haemoglobin and reticulocytes are all low. Bone marrow biopsy shows a hypocellular, fatty marrow with no abnormal cells.
questions.q: Which best explains why all three cell lines are low?
o: Autoimmune destruction of mature red cells
Failure of pluripotent haematopoietic stem cells
Infiltration of marrow by leukaemic blasts
Peripheral destruction in an enlarged spleen
questions.e: Aplastic anaemia destroys or suppresses pluripotent stem cells, so red cells, white cells and platelets all fail, giving pancytopenia.

steps.x: A science question: explain the finding with the underlying mechanism.
Empty marrow with pancytopenia.

elim: Would give isolated anaemia with reticulocytosis.
The marrow shows no abnormal cells.
The marrow would be hypercellular.
Would cause only anaemia, not pancytopenia.

steps.x: **B. Failure of pluripotent haematopoietic stem cells.** Aplastic = stem cell failure = pancytopenia.

questions.stem: A 70 year old man with sepsis develops bleeding from his cannula sites. Platelets are 34 ×10⁹/L (150–400), PT and APTT are prolonged, fibrinogen is low and D-dimer is very high. His blood film shows fragmented red cells.
questions.q: Which best explains the fragmented red cells?
o: Shearing on fibrin strands in small vessels
questions.e: In DIC (like TTP and HUS), red cells are mechanically sheared as they pass through vessels part-blocked by fibrin and platelet microthrombi, forming schistocytes.

steps.x: A science question: explain the finding with the underlying mechanism.
Microthrombi in small vessels cut red cells.

elim: Gives spherocytes.
Gives bite cells in G6PD deficiency.
Gives ring sideroblasts or megaloblasts.
Hereditary spherocytosis.

steps.x: **E. Shearing on fibrin strands in small vessels.** Schistocytes = mechanical shearing (TTP, HUS, DIC, valves).

questions.stem: A 16 year old girl of Irish descent has hereditary spherocytosis. Her father and paternal grandfather have the condition, and her brother is also affected. Her mother is unaffected. She asks how the condition is passed on.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mode of inheritance?
questions.e: Hereditary spherocytosis is usually autosomal dominant, more common in Northern Europeans; each child has a 1 in 2 chance.

steps.x: A science question: explain the finding with the underlying mechanism.
Every generation, both sexes, father-to-son transmission.

elim: Would not usually affect three generations in a row.
Passed only through the mother, never from a father.
Fathers cannot pass an X-linked gene to their sons, yet her brother is affected.
Father-to-son transmission and an affected girl exclude it.

steps.x: **A. Autosomal dominant.** HS = autosomal dominant.

questions.stem: A 4 year old boy has episodes of jaundice and dark urine after infections. His maternal uncle had similar episodes after eating fava beans. His mother and sister are well. His DAT is negative and red cell enzyme testing confirms the diagnosis.
questions.q: Which is the mode of inheritance?
questions.e: G6PD deficiency is X-linked recessive: males are affected through carrier mothers. G6PD normally makes NADPH to regenerate glutathione, protecting red cells from oxidative stress.

steps.x: A science question: explain the finding with the underlying mechanism.
Affected males linked through a healthy mother.

elim: Would show in every generation, including women.
Does not explain affected males linked through the mother.
Would affect all children of an affected mother.
His mother would be affected.

steps.x: **E. X-linked recessive.** G6PD deficiency = X-linked recessive.

questions.stem: A 29 year old woman has cold autoimmune haemolytic anaemia after Mycoplasma infection. Her MCV is 106 fL (80–100) and reticulocytes are 9% (0.5–2.5). Serum B12 and folate are normal. A junior doctor wants to start B12 injections.
questions.q: Which best explains her raised MCV?
questions.e: Reticulocytes are larger than mature red cells, so a brisk marrow response to haemolysis raises the MCV; in cold AIHA a new macrocytosis reflects reticulocytosis, not B12 or folate deficiency.

steps.x: A science question: explain the finding with the underlying mechanism.
Macrocytosis with a high reticulocyte count and normal vitamins.

elim: No history of drinking.
Folate is normal.
Not suggested by the history.
B12 is normal; injections are not needed.

steps.x: **D. Reticulocytosis.** Haemolysis can raise the MCV through retics.
